key_points.point: AI is already significantly boosting the speed and efficiency of research, allowing scientists to navigate massive problem spaces like protein folding at speeds previously impossible.
key_points.verbatim: Using these tools, researchers are able to navigate incredibly large problem spaces with greater ease and far greater speed. For instance, Google DeepMind’s AlphaFold can run through a vast number of ways proteins might be assembled and interact.

key_points.point: AI acts as a powerful assistant that automates time-intensive information gathering and synthesis, allowing human researchers to focus on higher-level inquiry and idea generation.
key_points.verbatim: “While these systems compile existing knowledge rather than generating novel insights, they speed up an important part of the research process by automating the time-intensive work of information gathering and initial synthesis.”

key_points.point: The author suggests that AI tools can be used to build vibrant, early-stage research tools that would have previously taken years to develop, significantly accelerating the research process.
key_points.verbatim: This kind of digital project would have previously taken years of effort at a digital humanities center; with tools like Claude Code, one can imagine quickly producing such a vibrant early-stage research tool for a single dissertation or article.

key_points.point: AI models are showing rapid, exponential improvement on complex academic benchmarks, demonstrating that scaling compute and data leads to significantly higher performance.
key_points.verbatim: The best LLMs had already surpassed me, and now, a year later, the latest models are roughly three times as able as they were a year ago on that same exam, still far from perfect but capable of producing accurate answers to very tough questions from the full range of academic disciplines.

key_points.point: The author envisions a future where AI systems are more flexible and expansive, similar to how the World Wide Web evolved to allow anyone to assemble new services and ideas.
key_points.verbatim: We may very well look back on our first years of engagement with AI in forms like ChatGPT as we now look back on AOL before the flourishing of the World Wide Web — a comfortable, contained, and relatively inflexible introduction to a new digital world.

key_points.point: AI-augmented research may be contracting science's reach by automating established fields and focusing on data-rich areas, potentially creating systemic blind spots.
key_points.verbatim: [The] adoption of AI in science presents what seems to be a paradox: an expansion of individual scientists’ impact but a contraction in collective science’s reach, as AI-augmented work moves collectively towards areas richest in data.

key_points.point: The author warns that AI tools are currently designed to narrow focus and summarize, which is the opposite of what is needed to spark new, open-ended research questions.
key_points.verbatim: This would be the opposite of AI’s current inclination toward summarization and constant narrowing.

key_points.point: Current AI systems are structurally designed as 'answer-machines' that struggle to engage in the open-ended, curious inquiry necessary for true scientific breakthroughs.
key_points.verbatim: Structurally and interface-wise, Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini are mostly answer-machines for our questions right now. Yes, they can ask us questions in response to our prompts, reversing the polarity briefly, but they are designed to be on the A side of Q&A.

key_points.point: There is a significant risk that AI-augmented work will automate established fields rather than exploring new ones, highlighting a tension between personal advancement and collective scientific progress.
key_points.verbatim: With reduced follow-on engagement, AI tools seem to automate established fields rather than explore new ones, highlighting a tension between personal advancement and collective scientific progress.

key_points.point: The author suggests that we need to design AI systems that surprise scholars and highlight the unusual, rather than just providing perfect alignment with existing search queries.
key_points.verbatim: But it might be worth surprising scholars from time to time rather than always giving them perfect alignment. This surprise could take the form of a sidebar of items that wouldn’t show up in a standard Boolean search.

key_points.point: The author argues that AI is best understood as a powerful tool that will be slowly integrated into existing work modes, rather than a revolutionary force that changes everything overnight.
key_points.verbatim: (Note that AI as “normal science” is different from, but not entirely unrelated to, AI as “normal technology,” a parallel critique suggesting that AI, while an extremely powerful tool, will be slowly integrated into modes of knowledge work we already understand, rather than revolutionizing them.)

key_points.point: AI-assisted research may be polluting scientific data by embedding biases and flaws from training data into future research, threatening the reliability of scientific studies.
key_points.verbatim: Researchers are starting to use AI to help them analyze data, but this creates a hidden problem. The AI’s own flaws and biases can get mixed into the research data, tainting it without anyone realizing.

key_points.point: The author emphasizes that human beings still have plenty of ways to conceive new ideas that don't use AI, such as interpersonal interaction and reading books.
key_points.verbatim: We human beings can find ourselves thinking new things simply by having coffee with another person, or by reading a good book they wrote.

key_points.point: The author notes that AI models are trained on existing data, which means they absorb and amplify existing biases, potentially automating established inequities in the scientific establishment.
key_points.verbatim: AI-generated hypotheses are only as good as the data they’re trained on, and that data reflects decades of structural inequality in who gets funded, who gets published, and whose problems get studied.

key_points.point: The author suggests that we should focus on the 'normal science' of puzzle-solving within existing conceptual frameworks, rather than assuming AI will revolutionize scientific discovery.
key_points.verbatim: In short, AI progress in some areas of research is impressive but nevertheless part of what the historian and philosopher of science Thomas Kuhn called “normal science,” the important work of filling out existing models and answering lingering questions through careful experiments and studies

factual_claims.claim: AI models have shown significant improvement on PhD-level comprehensive exams over the past year, moving from failing to producing accurate answers.
Google DeepMind’s AlphaFold can predict over 200 million protein structures.
A study in Nature found that AI adoption in science expands individual impact but contracts collective scientific reach by focusing on data-rich areas.

unmapped_concepts.suggested_description: The perspective that AI is a tool that will be slowly integrated into existing work modes rather than revolutionizing them. It frames AI as an incremental addition to current knowledge work.
unmapped_concepts.concept: The author references this as a parallel critique to 'normal science,' suggesting AI will be slowly integrated into modes of knowledge work we already understand, rather than revolutionizing them.
unmapped_concepts.reason: This concept provides a specific framing for AI adoption that contrasts with the revolutionary 'accelerationist' narrative.

unmapped_concepts.suggested_description: The inherent design bias of current LLMs toward providing answers rather than facilitating inquiry. It suggests that current AI architectures may be fundamentally ill-suited for the early stages of research where question formulation is more important than answer retrieval.
unmapped_concepts.concept: The author argues that current LLMs are structurally designed to be on the 'A side of Q&A,' making them poorly designed to prompt users to conceive new research questions.
unmapped_concepts.reason: This concept identifies a fundamental architectural limitation of current AI that impacts all POV camps' views on AI's role in research.
unmapped_concepts.Accelerationist Interpretation: This is a temporary architectural limitation that will be overcome as models evolve to handle more complex, multi-step reasoning and iterative dialogue.
unmapped_concepts.Safetyist Interpretation: This limitation is a safety feature, as it keeps the AI within a defined, answer-providing role, preventing it from autonomously formulating potentially dangerous or misaligned research agendas.
unmapped_concepts.Skeptic Interpretation: This confirms that AI is a pattern-matching tool, not an intelligent agent, and that its inability to engage in genuine inquiry is a fundamental limitation that should prevent us from over-relying on it for research.

unmapped_concepts.suggested_description: The phenomenon where organizations fund numerous low-cost, isolated AI pilots but fail to scale them due to a lack of infrastructure, integration, and strategic roadmap. It explains the gap between AI experimentation and enterprise-wide transformation.
unmapped_concepts.concept: The author alludes to this by noting that while AI tools are impressive, they are often integrated into existing modes of work rather than revolutionizing them, and that scaling these tools requires more than just the AI itself.
unmapped_concepts.reason: This concept addresses the practical, organizational challenges of AI adoption that are often ignored in the hype.
